opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's been a really interesting journey. When I joined Nvidia about ten years ago, most people still thought of us as a graphics card company, a gaming company. AI was there, but it wasn't yet the center of everything. Watching the company go from that to where it is today taught me a few things.

The first is about long-term conviction. Jensen made bets that didn't make sense to a lot of people at the time. CUDA is the classic example. For years the company invested in making GPUs general-purpose computing platforms when the market wasn't really asking for it, and it cost a lot. But the belief was that accelerated computing would matter, and when deep learning arrived, the platform was ready. So one lesson for me is that building a company is not just reacting to what customers want today. You have to have a view of where computing is going and be willing to invest before the payoff is obvious.

The second is that it's a full-stack problem. Nvidia doesn't think of itself as just a chip company. It's the chips, the systems, the networking, the software libraries, the frameworks, and increasingly the models. In research, we feel this directly. When we build something like a world foundation model for physical AI, we're not only thinking about the algorithm. We're thinking about how developers will use it, how it runs on the hardware, what the data pipeline looks like. Real impact comes when the whole stack works together.

The third is about culture. Nvidia is quite flat and very transparent. Information moves fast, and people are expected to work on the most important problems, not to protect their territory. Jensen often talks about the speed of light, meaning: what's the best possible outcome if there were no excuses, and how close can we get? That mindset pushes everyone to think from first principles instead of incrementally.

And finally, I'd say resilience. People see the success now, but there were many hard periods: products that didn't work, markets that didn't materialize, moments when the stock was way down. The company survived because it kept learning and kept reinventing itself. For me, that's maybe the deepest lesson: a great company isn't one that never fails, it's one that can keep transforming while staying true to a core belief.

r001.rationale: The response describes Nvidia’s shift from graphics and gaming toward AI and says the payoff from CUDA was not obvious, but it does not clearly say that the transformation was difficult to foresee from inside the company.

r002.rationale: It describes years of investment in CUDA based on a long-term belief, continuing before the payoff was clear, and learning and reinventing through hard periods.

r003.rationale: It says Nvidia’s culture encourages first-principles thinking, but does not connect that reasoning to choosing the company’s goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I joined Nvidia around 2016, it was still mostly thought of as a gaming company. GPUs were for graphics. A lot of people I talked to in academia asked me why I would go there instead of a place that was "really" doing AI. And then over ten years I watched it become the company that essentially powers the whole AI wave. That changed how I think about building anything.

The first lesson is that a company's identity is not fixed by what it currently sells. Nvidia bet on parallel computing long before there was a clear market for it. CUDA existed for years as something that mostly cost money. Jensen kept investing because he believed accelerated computing was inevitable, even when the quarterly numbers didn't justify it. So I learned that you build toward where the world is going, not where the revenue is today. You need conviction, and you need to be willing to look wrong for a long time.

The second lesson is about staying close to the technology. Nvidia is a very large company now, but the culture still rewards people who actually understand the details. Jensen reads papers. He'll ask engineers very specific questions. That taught me that leadership isn't abstracted management; it's being able to make judgment calls because you understand what's real and what's hype. When I lead research teams, I try to keep that. I want to know what the model is actually doing, not just read a slide about it.

The third lesson, maybe the most important for me, is about speed and the "mission is the boss" idea. At Nvidia we don't really have rigid org charts for projects. If something matters, people from different teams just form around it. Information flows very flat. That's how the company could pivot so fast when deep learning took off, and again when generative AI arrived. A company that's organized around protecting fiefdoms can't do that. A company organized around the mission can.

And I'd add one more thing from my own experience in research. The transformation taught me that research only matters if it connects to a platform. We did a lot of work on generative models, image synthesis, simulation. Early on it was impressive demos. What made it meaningful was when it fed into products, into the full stack, into what developers could build. So when I think about building a company now, I think less about "what's the clever idea" and more about "what's the platform that lets a thousand other people build their clever ideas." That's really the Nvidia way, and watching it work at that scale, for ten years, is something I couldn't have learned anywhere else.

r001.rationale: It describes Nvidia as still seen mainly as a gaming company, with no clear market for parallel computing, before it became the company powering the AI wave.

r002.rationale: It says Jensen kept investing in CUDA for years despite weak near-term justification, guided by conviction that accelerated computing was inevitable.

r003.rationale: The response discusses conviction and building toward future demand, but does not say to choose a company goal through first-principles reasoning.

astra-6.text:
Looking back over those ten years, what stands out to me is that building a company means continually building the capability to do something new. You need to execute on what matters today, but you also need to invest in things whose value may not be obvious yet. And you need a way for those long-term investments to become part of the business when the opportunity arrives.

That has shaped how I think about focus. Focus doesn’t necessarily mean staying with the same product forever. It means having a clear sense of what you’re uniquely good at, while being willing to rethink where that capability can take you. As the company grows, the challenge is to keep that willingness to learn—to make sure past success doesn’t become the reason you stop changing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Nvidia’s changing capabilities but does not say its eventual association with AI was difficult to foresee.

r002.rationale: It describes ongoing capability-building and long-term investment, but does not frame company building as incremental work toward a goal one believes in.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss choosing a company goal through first-principles reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back over those ten years, what stands out to me is that building a company means continually developing the ability to do something new. The products change, the opportunities change, and the organization has to learn along the way.

You need a long-term direction, but you also need the flexibility to change how you get there. That’s a difficult balance. If you only focus on the immediate business, it’s hard to invest in something whose value isn’t clear yet. But a long-term vision also has to translate into concrete work that teams can execute today.

So that experience shaped how I think about company building: you’re building both a product and a team that can keep learning together. The second part is what allows the company to evolve beyond its first success.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing products and opportunities, but does not say Nvidia’s rise as a globally recognized AI company was difficult to foresee.

r002.rationale: It describes continually learning and developing new capabilities, guided by a long-term direction and translated into concrete work teams can do today.

r003.rationale: It recommends having a long-term direction, but does not say to choose the company’s goal through first-principles reasoning.
